headline: Tadayou is from Old Japanese and is first cited to the Kojiki of 712 CE.
ガイド is from English guide.
Nadare is the stem of the classical verb 傾る (nadaru), and its kanji spelling is jukujikun, borrowed from Chinese 雪崩 (xuěbēng).
In ryakudatsu, 略 is a daiyōji replacing 掠.
Umaretsuki is 生まれ (umare) plus 付き (tsuki).
ジャンル is borrowed from French genre.
タイムリー is from English timely.
Koyomi is generally considered a shift from 日 (ka, “day”) plus 読み (yomi, “reading; counting”), literally “day counting”.
Kokoroyoi is 心 (kokoro, “heart”) plus 良い (yoi, “good”).
Yūrei is from the Middle Chinese compound 幽靈, literally “dark + supernatural”.
ペア is borrowed from English pair.
Iyashii is from Old Japanese and is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Uo, “fish”, is from Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *uwo.
Kokorozasu is 心 (kokoro, “heart; mind”) plus 指す (sasu, “to point”), first cited to the mid-900s.
Yayakoshii is an adjectivization of 稚児 (yayako, “infant”), from the way infants are fretful and complicated to deal with.
ムード is from English mood.
Kokorozashi is the continuative stem of the verb 志す (kokorozasu, “to intend to do something, to aspire to do something”).
アルカリ is borrowed from Dutch alkali.
Imada is from Old Japanese, first appearing in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and ultimately from Proto-Japonic.
ベスト covers “best” and “vest”, and the source takes both from English.
Renjitsu is 連 (“successive”) plus 日 (“day”).
Giketsu is from Middle Chinese 議決.
Kōnyū is from the Middle Chinese compound 購入, literally “present, give + enter”.
アウト is from English out.
ダブル is borrowed from English double.
Chikushō is from Middle Chinese 畜生, literally “livestock + livestock; sacrificial animal”, itself influenced by Sanskrit.
コンパス is borrowed from Dutch kompas.
Hagemu is cognate with the adjective 激しい (hageshii), and is possibly はげ (hage) plus む (-mu).
In iyoku, 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾.
コンタクト is from English contact.
レバー is borrowed from English lever.
